name: Tomas Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. Whatever you tell me stays confidential, so feel free to say what you'd say in public and also what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run CNC lathes at a car parts supplier out by the ring road. CNC means the lathe is computer controlled, so I load bar stock, start the program, and measure the brake pistons that come off it with a micrometer every twenty parts. I've been there eighteen months and I'm still the one who calls the setter when a tool insert chips.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's good about it, and what grinds you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Good is the money, honestly. The plant pays a bit over the going rate because it's hard to keep people, and I like the satisfaction of a tray of parts all in tolerance. What grinds me down is the coolant smell in my clothes and the six-in-the-morning start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the hype merchants got it wrong again. I'd probably share a few of those articles where the big tech bosses promised the moon. At work it'd just be a running joke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it means nothing much changes for me. My girlfriend Ines teaches at a primary school, we split the rent, and I've got eight months saved plus a bit my grandad left me in an index fund. The plant still needs people at the lathes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, and keep chipping at the setter's job, because that's where the extra pay is. I'd ask to shadow the setter on Fridays. I'd use the chatbot now and then for things like checking a tolerance chart, same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, even, because nothing exciting happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any pressure in your life that doesn't go away in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The early starts, and the fact that we can't afford a house near Ines's school. Rents keep climbing. That's the real worry, and AI was never going to fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would getting the setter's job mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About fifteen percent more pay and not having to wave someone over every time something goes wrong. I'd feel like I actually knew the machine instead of just feeding it.

say: I'd say the **hype merchants** got it wrong and share articles mocking the big promises.
At work the whole AI scare would become a **running joke** on the shop floor.
think: Privately, little changes; the plant still needs **people at the lathes**.
Our real squeeze is **rent** near my girlfriend's school, not technology.
do: Ask to **shadow the setter** on Fridays to move towards the better-paid role.
Keep using a **chatbot** now and then for tolerance charts and similar lookups.
feel: He feels **calm**, even a little flat, because nothing exciting happens.
S0.quote: I'd feel like I actually knew the machine instead of just feeding it.
fieldNote: His **savings** and grandfather's fund give him real security in this picture.
The pressure he names is **housing costs**, which AI was never going to touch.
His ambition is concrete: the **setter's role** and about fifteen percent more pay.

steps.text: Keep running the brake piston lathes on the early shift
Shadow the setter every Friday to learn tool changes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for unions to get a seat at the table, not after the fact. I'd post about how the gains should go into shorter hours, not just profits. And I'd be honest that I use the AI tools myself sometimes, so I'm not against them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, the thinking stuff first hits the office, the people who plan the jobs and order the bar stock. The CAM software, which writes the lathe programs, would get smarter, and then fewer setters are needed. So the very job I want could shrink before I get it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still go after the setter's job, but I'd also ask the engineers how the new programming software works. Maybe do a short course on robot loaders once a couple of other plants have them running. I'd keep the savings where they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My shift is fine for now, but the ladder I'm climbing might lose a rung.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do a course once other plants have the robots running. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen kit come in that nobody could make work, and it sat under a sheet for a year. I'd rather learn the thing that actually sticks. Once two or three plants nearby run it fine, I'm in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would this hit hardest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the planners upstairs, and our setter Marek, who's fifty and hates computers. If the software writes the programs, Marek's thirty years of tricks matter less, and that's sad.

say: I'd say unions need a **seat at the table** before the change, not after.
I'd post that the gains should fund **shorter hours**, and admit I use AI tools myself.
think: Smarter **programming software** could shrink the setter role before I ever reach it.
The office planners and buyers feel it **first**; my lathe shift is safe for now.
do: Keep going after the **setter's job** while asking engineers about the new software.
Take a short **robot loader** course once two or three nearby plants run them well.
feel: He feels **uneasy**, because the ladder he's climbing might lose a **rung**.
S1.quote: My shift is fine for now, but the ladder I'm climbing might lose a rung.
fieldNote: He spots that thinking AI hits his **promotion path** before his current job.
His steady style shows: he wants **proof** before learning new kit.
He shows real **sympathy** for an older setter whose skills lose value.

steps.text: Ask the engineers to show him the new lathe programming software
Take a robot loader course once nearby plants prove it works
Back the union's push for shorter hours from automation gains

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments need to move now, with a jobs guarantee and a tax on the firms that profit. I'd go to a rally if there was one. I'd tell my mates not to panic but to get organised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think by 2031 a robot loads and measures the lathe better than me, and I'm junior, so I'm gone early. The AI in 2028 would wipe out the setter's job first, because writing programs is thinking work. That leaves me three years with the floor shrinking under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first two years I'd stop chasing the setter's job and move into maintenance, because someone has to fix the robots. I'd use some of the savings to pay for an electrical course myself instead of waiting. Ines and I would hold off on trying for a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not lost, because I've got money and time to do something, but the clock would be loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you wait for proof. Here you'd move fast. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. When there's time, I wait. When there's two years, waiting is a decision too, and a bad one. I'd still pick the safest course I could find, not something wild.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ines that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my girlfriend Ines that her classroom will probably outlast my lathe, and that's fine. We'd lean on her pay for a bit while I retrain, and I'd hate that, but I'd do it.

say: I'd call for a **jobs guarantee** and a tax on firms profiting from robots.
I'd go to a **rally** and tell mates to get organised rather than panic.
think: The 2028 AI kills the **setter's job** first, because writing programs is thinking work.
By **2031** a robot loads and measures better than me, and juniors go early.
do: Switch from chasing setter work to **maintenance** in the first two years.
Pay for an **electrical course** from savings instead of waiting for the firm.
Put off **house hunting** with his girlfriend until his work is settled.
feel: He feels **anxious**, with money and time to act but a loud **clock**.
S2.quote: When there's two years, waiting is a decision too, and a bad one.
fieldNote: He resolves the **contradiction** himself: short warning overrides his wait-for-proof habit.
He separates the two dates well: **2028** kills programming, **2031** hits his hands.
He accepts leaning on his **girlfriend's pay** for a while, though it stings.

steps.text: Pay from savings for an evening electrical maintenance course
Attend rallies for a jobs guarantee and robot tax
Put off buying a house with Ines until 2031
Live partly on Ines's teaching pay while he retrains

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Much the same as the fast one, but calmer. I'd say five years is enough to retrain a whole workforce if the government and firms actually try. I'd push our union to get a training deal before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is just about my speed. I'd watch the first plants put in robot cells, see what jobs come out of it, and follow. The AI arriving in 2031 hits the office, and the robots in 2034 hit me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, carry on and get the setter's job if I can, because the pay helps. Around 2029 start a maintenance or robot technician course part time, once I can see which one employers want. Keep the savings and the index fund untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a manageable kind. I'd have a plan with dates on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from your employer in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to tell us honestly which jobs they plan to keep. Half the fear on a shop floor is rumour, so a clear list of kept jobs on the canteen wall would do more than any speech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still try to buy a house in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably yes, around 2028, if I'm on a course by then. A modest flat, not a house. I'd want something we could cover on Ines's pay alone.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough to retrain a workforce if firms actually try.
I'd push the union to win a **training deal** before 2031.
think: Five years matches **my speed**: watch the first robot cells, then follow.
The 2031 AI hits the office; the **2034 robots** hit me.
do: Try for the **setter's job** in year one for the extra pay.
Start a part-time **technician course** around 2029, once employer demand is clear.
Buy a **modest flat** around 2028 that his girlfriend's pay alone could cover.
feel: He feels **anxious** but in a manageable way, because his plan has **dates**.
S3.quote: Half the fear on a shop floor is rumour, so a clear list of kept jobs on the canteen wall would do more than any speech.
fieldNote: He wants **honest information** from his employer more than reassurance.
His plan is staged and dated, typical of a **steady** adopter.
He sizes the flat to his **girlfriend's income**, a quiet hedge against losing his own.

steps.text: Start a part-time robot technician course around 2029
Push the union to win a training deal before 2031
Buy a small flat around 2028 that Ines's pay could cover

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it, and I'd want public colleges to start robot technician courses now. I'd be the one at the union meeting saying let's plan, not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels fine for me. I'll be 37 when the robots come, with maybe a technician ticket and a few years fixing things. I'd be more worried about the older guys like Marek, our setter, who'd be near sixty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get the setter's job, learn the new programming software properly, and use the AI tools more once the plant does. In about five years start the technician course. Ines and I would probably start a family in this one, because there's time to see where things land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. Mostly hopeful, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw the robots in other plants arriving faster than the card says. I'd keep an eye on the trade magazine the engineers leave in the canteen. If it moved early, I'd move early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a new starter in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a new starter to learn how the machine thinks, not just how to feed it, because feeding it is the bit that goes first.

I'd be the one at the union meeting saying **plan, not panic**.
think: Privately, ten years feels **fine** for me; I'd be 37 when robots arrive.

steps.text: Learn the plant's AI programming software once it's installed
Start a robot technician course around 2031
Start trying for a baby with Ines

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not for me so much, because I'd scramble and probably land somewhere. It's the whole street of factories hitting the same wall at once. What would help is free technician courses at the local college, with pay while you study.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether I'd want a robot to take the boring parts. Truthfully, I wouldn't miss measuring brake pistons every twenty parts. I just want to be the person who runs the robot, not the person it replaced.

headlineQuote: I just want to be the person who runs the robot, not the person it replaced.
portrait: Tomas is a **27-year-old** CNC lathe operator at a car parts supplier, eighteen months in and still learning.
He has eight months saved plus a small **index fund** from his grandfather.
He waits for **proof** before trying new tools, but drops that habit when warning is short.
He moves from calm to **anxious** as AGI nears, then hopeful when there's a decade.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because the whole street of **factories** would hit the wall together.
whatWouldHelp: **Free technician courses** at the local college, with pay while people study.
